# Diagnosing P0100 and EVAP Vacuum Issues After Air Filter Replacement

Replacing an air filter in a 2000 Nissan Super Saloon (N16) is a routine maintenance task, but it often triggers specific sensor logic errors if the airflow path isn't managed correctly. The sequence you described—installing a new filter, triggering the Check Engine Light (CEL), and subsequently seeing power loss—strongly suggests an interruption in the Mass Airflow (MAF) signal or a physical blockage of the sensor itself.

When you installed the new filter, it is highly probable that oil residue from the old filter media coated the MAF sensor rods inside the housing. Modern ECUs rely on precise voltage readings from the MAF to calculate fuel injection timing. If the sensor output drops below the expected threshold due to debris or improper sealing, the ECU throws a P0100 code (MAF System Malfunction). This causes the engine to run "open loop," ignoring the faulty sensor data and defaulting to a rich mixture, which results in the noticeable power loss you experienced.

The fact that the light went off after cycling the ignition keys indicates the ECU performed a self-test on startup and temporarily cleared the stored fault code because the condition appeared resolved at that exact moment. However, once you drove and the engine conditions changed—likely creating enough airflow to disturb the contaminated sensor or exposing a vacuum leak—the P0100 re-triggered.

You mentioned suspecting oil residue stuck to the MAF rods. While blowing compressed air is better than brushing with a rag (which can damage delicate wires), it often fails if the sensor element was fully submerged in old filter dust. The definitive fix for this specific scenario involves cleaning the sensor head with MAF-specific cleaner or, more reliably, swapping the entire MAF sensor assembly. You noted replacing the sensor but the light remaining on; this confirms that while P0100 is definitely involved, it may not be the *only* issue present, or the replacement part has a compatibility variance with your specific N16 engine management system.

Your second observation regarding the fuel tank lid depressurizing with a vacuum sound points toward an Evaporative Emission Control (EVAP) system malfunction. The EVAP system is designed to capture fuel vapors and store them in a charcoal canister, venting them only when the engine creates positive crankcase pressure or during specific drive cycles. A sudden vacuum pull on the tank suggests a clogged purge valve preventing equalization, or potentially a breach in the lines creating an unintended leak that the ECU interprets as a system fault. This could be a secondary code (like P045x) masked by the more critical M0100 error.

Without a live OBD scanner to view real-time data streams, diagnosing these two concurrent issues is difficult. The vacuum sound on the tank lid warrants checking the EVAP purge solenoid and associated hoses for kinks or blockages. If you cannot access a shop immediately, verify that all air filter housing gaskets are seated perfectly; even a slight misalignment can create a false "dirty MAF" reading by allowing unmetered air to bypass the sensor.

If the new MAF sensor still yields P0100 after clearing codes and driving for 20 minutes, you may need to inspect the wiring harness connector for corrosion or loose pins. Sometimes the issue is not the sensor itself but a poor electrical connection that becomes intermittent under vibration.
